title: The Morning Brief: Federal cases, settlement expansion, and infrastructure strain reshape the week
dek: The morning brings federal charges against a New York woman plotting a Capitol attack, an FBI seizure in an investigation of former Rep. Swalwell, and a defamation verdict against the New York Times. Internationally, Russia strikes Kyiv's infrastructure, Israel advances settlement construction ahead of elections, and the Panama Canal cuts traffic due to drought.
author: GoCheckMyNews
key_fact: The day is split between domestic legal escalations, from terrorism allegations to defamation damages, and foreign policy pressures: Russian strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure, Israeli settlement expansion tied to October elections, and a critical trade bottleneck tightening due to climate disruption.
bottom_line: Three strands run through the morning: federal law enforcement escalating cases tied to domestic extremism and official misconduct, foreign powers testing resolve in Ukraine and the Middle East with elections on the horizon, and critical infrastructure under climate and geopolitical strain. The coming days will test whether the Swalwell investigation moves toward charges, whether Israel's October election changes the settlement pace, and whether Central American rainfall eases the Panama Canal bottleneck. Watch the September 15 canal capacity cut, October 19 Israeli settlement bid deadline, and October 26 Jeffries trial start date.
body: Jessica Bowie, 35, of Albany, New York, was apprehended on August 19 after obtaining what she believed to be an explosive device, according to a Justice Department charge sheet released this morning. She faces federal counts for attempting to provide material support to ISIS and plotting to deploy that device at the New York State Capitol with the intent to kill public officials and destroy the building before fleeing to ISIS-controlled territory in Syria. The FBI investigation involved confidential sources and surveillance. Meanwhile, federal agents executed search warrants on former Democratic Rep. Eric Swalwell's residence and seized an iPhone and MacBook Pro as part of a criminal investigation into sexual misconduct allegations. Swalwell resigned from Congress in April following a House Ethics Committee inquiry; investigators are examining potential charges under a federal statute making it a crime for officials to deprive individuals of constitutional rights. The investigation remains ongoing with no announced timeline for charges.

In civil litigation, an Alabama jury awarded $9.25 million in damages to Kai Spears, a former walk-on for the University of Alabama men's basketball team, after finding the New York Times defamed him by falsely reporting he was present at a fatal 2023 shooting in Tuscaloosa. The verdict marks the Times' first defamation loss on a published article in over 50 years. The newspaper had reported Spears was in a car struck by bullets during a January 15, 2023 shooting; Spears sued in 2023 after the article's publication. The honest read on the sourcing is that the verdict exposes a rare vulnerability for major news outlets when factual reporting on crime involves false claims about an identified individual's presence or knowledge of events; what remains to be determined is whether the Times appeals and how a higher court addresses the legal reasoning underlying the jury's finding.

Abroad, Russia struck Kyiv around midnight with missiles and drones, killing at least 17 people and injuring more than 40, according to Ukraine's State Emergency Service. A children's hospital, school, apartment blocks, and warehouses were damaged; power was cut to thousands of properties across the region. The Ukrainian Air Force reported that none of the Russian ballistic missiles used in the overnight attack were intercepted. The strike marks the first time in several months that critical infrastructure in the capital was purposefully targeted, according to Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko. The attack compounds Ukraine's winter vulnerability as Russia targets heat and power infrastructure.

In the occupied West Bank, Israel re-established the Kadim settlement with 30 families on Thursday, completing the reversal of all four settlements evacuated in 2005 during the Disengagement Plan. The move comes as Israel's housing ministry opened construction tenders for roughly 1,234 settlement homes in the E1 area between East Jerusalem and the settlement of Maale Adumim, with bids due October 19, days before Israel's October 27 election. Five Western democracies, the UK, France, Germany, Italy, and Canada, issued a joint statement calling Israel's settlement tender "unacceptable" and urging immediate withdrawal. The October 19 tender deadline precedes Israel's October 27 election, placing settlement expansion at the center of domestic political calculation.

The Panama Canal Authority announced Thursday that it will cut daily vessel traffic from 36 to 32 ships starting September 15, citing low rainfall caused by El Niño. The reduction, phased in from September 3, affects one of the world's most critical trade chokepoints at a moment when global shipping already faces severe disruptions from conflict in the Middle East.

Other developments: The Justice Department announced a $400 million settlement with TikTok and ByteDance resolving litigation over alleged violations of the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act. TikTok will pay $300 million immediately, with an additional $100 million contingent on vacating a prior consent decree related to Musical.ly. Federal Judge Nusrat Choudhury ruled that former Abercrombie & Fitch CEO Mike Jeffries is competent to stand trial on sex trafficking charges, reversing an earlier finding of mental incompetence; trial is scheduled to begin on October 26. The Pentagon fired Stars and Stripes publisher Max Lederer, editor-in-chief Erik Slavin, and reporter Lara Korte on Friday, citing insubordination over unauthorized participation in a CBS Sunday Morning segment. Chief Justice John Roberts issued a temporary stay allowing President Trump's White House ballroom construction to proceed, blocking lower court orders that would have halted the above-ground portion of the $400 million project. A Texas appellate court cut a $50 million judgment against Alex Jones to $1.5 million, finding Sandy Hook parents did not show evidence that harassment exceeded Texas's damage cap; a separate $1.4 billion Connecticut judgment remains unchanged. The Interior Department mandated a 1.25 million acre-feet annual water reduction for California, Nevada, and Arizona beginning in 2027, with Arizona losing 760,000 acre-feet.
